# Modern C++ for Performance: RAII, Move Semantics, Stack Allocation ## Overview Trading and AI infra systems demand low latency. C++ offers: 1. **RAII** (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization): deterministic cleanup, zero-cost abstractions 2. **Move semantics**: avoid unnecessary copies, perfect forwarding 3. **Stack allocation**: predictable latency (no malloc), cache locality 4. **Smart pointers**: automatic memory management without garbage collection overhead This lesson covers the mental models behind C++ performance, not syntax drills. --- ## RAII: Ownership and Determinism **Problem:** Manual memory management (malloc/free, new/delete) is error-prone. ```cpp // Bad: manual cleanup void process_order(Order* o) { Buffer* buf = new Buffer(1024); if (o->is_valid()) { // ... use buf } delete buf; // What if we return early? Exception? } // Good: RAII void process_order(const Order& o) { Buffer buf(1024); // ctor: allocate if (o.is_valid()) { // ... use buf } // dtor: deallocate (automatic, even on exception) } ``` **Key:** In C++, object lifetime = resource lifetime. When the object goes out of scope, the destructor runs. No manual cleanup needed. **Guarantees:** - Exception-safe: if you throw, the dtor still runs (stack unwinding). - Predictable: allocation/deallocation happen at known points in code. - Zero-cost: the compiler inlines the dtor, no runtime overhead. **RAII in practice:** ```cpp // Lock guard (mutex is acquired in ctor, released in dtor) { std::lock_guard lock(mutex_); // Critical section } // dtor runs here, mutex released (exception-safe!) // Unique pointer (owns the allocation, dtor deletes it) std::unique_ptr o = std::make_unique(...); // o.get() returns the pointer; when o goes out of scope, memory freed ``` **Interview angle:** Why is RAII better than try/finally? - Answer: RAII is automatic (compiler enforces it), try/finally is manual (you can forget). RAII works with exceptions, RAII works with early returns. --- ## Move Semantics and Perfect Forwarding **Problem:** Copying is expensive. ```cpp std::vector orders; Order large_order = Order{...lots of data...}; orders.push_back(large_order); // Copy! O(n) memory transfer ``` **Solution:** Move semantics. If the source is a temporary (rvalue), steal its resources instead of copying. ```cpp std::vector orders; Order large_order = Order{...lots of data...}; orders.push_back(std::move(large_order)); // Move! Swap pointers, O(1) // large_order is now in a "moved-from" state (no longer usable) ``` **How it works:** ```mermaid graph LR A["Order obj1
(owns buffer)"] B["std::move
(cast to rvalue ref)"] C["Order obj2
(now owns buffer)"] D["obj1
(empty state)"] A -->|move ctor| C A -->|leaves in| D style A fill:#fff4e6 style C fill:#e8f5e9 style D fill:#ffcdd2 ``` **Rvalue reference (`&&`):** ```cpp // Copy constructor (lvalue ref) Order(const Order& other) { /* deep copy */ } // Move constructor (rvalue ref) Order(Order&& other) { /* steal resources */ } // Move assignment Order& operator=(Order&& other) { /* steal, release old */ } ``` **Perfect forwarding (generic templates):** ```cpp template void store(T&& obj) { // Accepts both lvalues and rvalues container.push_back(std::forward(obj)); // Forward as-is } Order o; store(o); // Binds to lvalue, copied store(Order{...}); // Binds to rvalue, moved ``` **Interview angle:** When do you use `std::move`? - Answer: Only on temporaries or objects you're done with. Using `std::move` on an object you still use is undefined behavior (moved-from state is valid but unpredictable). --- ## Stack Allocation and Cache Locality **Problem:** Heap allocation is variable latency. ```cpp // Heap allocation (slow path) Order* o = new Order(); // malloc: may trigger page refill (~10 us spike) // indirection: cpu cache miss on access // free: same latency problem // Stack allocation (fast, predictable) Order o; // 100+ bytes on stack, no malloc call // Access: likely in L1/L2 cache (4–10 ns) // Cleanup: automatic, no free() call ``` **Cache hierarchy (H100 GPU, but same principle on CPU):** ```mermaid graph TD A["Data in main memory"] B["L3 cache
30–50 ns latency
8–20 MB"] C["L2 cache
10–20 ns latency
256 KB per core"] D["L1 cache
4–10 ns latency
32 KB per core"] E["CPU registers
1 ns latency"] A -->|miss| B B -->|miss| C C -->|miss| D D -->|hit| E style E fill:#c8e6c9 style D fill:#fff9c4 style C fill:#ffccbc style B fill:#ffcdd2 style A fill:#f5f5f5 ``` **Stack vs heap: latency profile** ``` Stack allocation (first 1000 allocations): Allocation 1–1000: ~0 ns (just bump a pointer) Access: 4–10 ns (in L1 cache) Deallocation: ~0 ns (just bump pointer back) Heap allocation: Allocation 1: ~20 ns (allocator finds free block) Allocation 100: ~30 ns (same) Allocation 101: ~10 us (page refill, memcpy) Access: 50–100 ns (indirection + L3 miss) Deallocation: ~50 ns (allocator bookkeeping) ``` **Rule of thumb:** - **Stack:** Objects < ~1 MB, known at compile time, accessed frequently. - **Heap:** Large objects, dynamic sizing, long-lived (across function calls). **RAII on the stack:** ```cpp void match_order(const Order& buy, const Order& sell) { std::vector fills; // Stack allocation, size pre-reserved fills.reserve(100); // Allocates heap, but once // Process fills (fills.data() pointer never changes) for (int i = 0; i < buy.qty; ++i) { fills.push_back({buy.id, sell.id, 1}); } // dtor runs here, vector freed } ``` --- ## Profiling: perf, flamegraph, Instruments **Interview angle:** How do you prove a performance claim? **Tool 1: perf (Linux)** ```bash perf record -F 99 ./order_book_engine # Sample at 99 Hz perf report # Top functions by wall-clock time ``` Output: Function name, % of time. Find where latency lives. **Tool 2: flamegraph (CPU time visualization)** ```bash perf record -F 99 -g ./order_book_engine perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > graph.svg ``` Visualization: tall stacks = slow functions, wide areas = common paths. **Tool 3: Instruments (macOS/iOS)** ```bash xcode-select --install instruments -t 'System Trace' ./app # Records CPU time, cache misses, context switches, I/O ``` **Real measurement strategy:** 1. Record with perf/Instruments for 10 sec (captures steady state, not startup noise). 2. Look at top 3 functions by wall-clock time (they often consume 70%+ of time). 3. Measure before/after optimization to prove impact. **Interview trap:** "It's fast because I use smart pointers" — No. Measure. Smart pointers are zero-cost *in the common path* (just pointer manipulation), but if you use them wrong (unnecessary copies, deep cloning), they're slow. --- ## Story Card: OrderBookEngine Lock-Free Move Semantics **Setup:** High-frequency order book in C++, targeting P99.9 < 5 us. **Decision 1:** Use `std::deque` to store FIFO orders per price level. But copying each Order (128 bytes) on every insertion was adding latency. **Fix:** Switch to `std::vector`, move-only semantics (`Order` has deleted copy ctor), pre-allocate the vector once at startup. **Result:** - Before: Allocation + copy: ~1 us per order - After: Allocation + move: ~0.1 us per order - P99.9 latency: improved from 8 us to 3–5 us **What changed:** - Learned that move semantics are not just syntactic; they are a *data structure* optimization. Choosing the right container (vector vs deque) matters more than the syntax. - Realized that pre-allocation (reserve) is orthogonal to move semantics; both matter. **In an interview:** - Q: "Why not use `std::list`? It has O(1) insert anywhere." - A: "std::list has pointer indirection (cache miss on every node access). Vector with move semantics is faster in practice despite occasional reallocations." --- ## Q&A **Recall 1:** Explain RAII in one sentence. Why is it better than try/finally? *Must-say:* - Object lifetime = resource lifetime; destructor runs automatically on scope exit, even on exception. - Try/finally requires manual cleanup code; RAII is compiler-enforced. **Probe 1:** You have a `std::unique_ptr o`. You pass it to a function `void process(Order* p)`. What happens? *Expected:* - `process(o.get())` passes the raw pointer to the function. - Function cannot delete the pointer (it doesn't own it). - When `o` goes out of scope, the unique_ptr's dtor deletes the memory. - This is safe: ownership is clear. *Mistake:* If you do `process(o.release())`, the function now owns the pointer, and leaking is your fault. **Probe 2:** You have a vector of Orders. You `push_back(order)`. Order has a deleted copy constructor. What happens? *Expected:* - If `order` is an lvalue, compilation fails (can't copy). - If `order` is an rvalue (temporary or `std::move(order)`), the move ctor runs, vector takes ownership. - This forces users to think about ownership. **Numeric 1:** A function allocates a 10 MB buffer on the heap. It's called 1000 times per second. What's the latency impact? *Working:* - Allocation: ~100 us (allocator finds free block, may trigger page refill) - Deallocation: ~50 us - Total: ~150 us per call - 1000 calls/sec = 150 ms per second of wall-clock time (significant!) *Optimization:* Pre-allocate once, reuse the buffer. **Numeric 2:** Cache miss latency: L1 hit = 4 ns, L3 miss = 50 ns. A loop touches 1000 random Order objects (128 bytes each, not in cache). Time per iteration? *Working:* - 1000 objects, 128 bytes each = 128 KB - Doesn't fit in L1 (32 KB) or L2 (256 KB), mostly L3 misses or main memory - L3 miss = 50 ns, main memory = 100 ns - Assume average 75 ns per object - 1000 * 75 ns = 75 us total loop --- ## Questions for the Interviewer - How does your team profile performance? (perf, custom instrumentation, flamegraph?) - Do you use pre-allocation and object pooling for latency-sensitive code? - How much do you rely on move semantics vs deep copying in your codebase? - Have you hit any RAII gotchas (exception safety, undefined behavior)?
